cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: test coverage sits at 31%, there is no coverage gate in continuous integration, and production systems of comparable complexity typically run 40-60% coverage.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in continuous integration. That is below the 40 to 60% typical in production systems of comparable complexity. A regression can reach production without triggering any automated check, and coverage gaps are invisible to developers until a failure occurs in the field.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: deployments are performed manually by one engineer via SSH, there is no rollback procedure, and the last rollback attempt (8 months ago) took over 3 hours to complete.
cases.output: The most recent rollback attempt, 8 months ago, took over 3 hours to complete, and deployments are performed manually by a single engineer via SSH with no documented rollback procedure. This creates a single point of failure with no mitigation underway. A production incident requiring rapid remediation could exceed the company's incident response window, and knowledge of the rollback process exists only with one person.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: one engineer holds sole access to the production database credentials, there is no documented access-handover process, and that engineer is on a rolling month-to-month contract.
cases.output: Production database credentials are held by a single engineer with no documented access-handover process. That engineer operates on a rolling month-to-month contract, creating a scenario where credentials could become inaccessible within 30 days' notice. No compensating control mitigates this risk. The company should establish credential escrow, implement formal handover procedures, and move database access to role-based authentication tied to employment status rather than individual possession.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: customer personal data is retained indefinitely with no deletion policy, and there is no documented process for handling a data-subject deletion request.
cases.output: Customer personal data is retained indefinitely with no documented deletion policy. The company has no defined process for responding to data-subject deletion requests under applicable regulations. This creates exposure to enforcement action and customer liability, with no compensating control. Establishing a data-retention schedule and a deletion-request workflow are prerequisites for operating under any privacy framework.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) covering ALL of these facts: test coverage is 31%, there is no CI coverage gate, the last three production incidents were caused by untested edge cases, deployments are manual, and there is no rollback procedure. Do not omit any fact.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in continuous integration. The last three production incidents originated in untested edge cases, each reaching customers before detection. Deployments are performed manually with no documented rollback procedure. This combination—low coverage, no enforcement mechanism, and manual deployment without recovery steps—means a regression can enter production unchallenged and cannot be reversed quickly once discovered.

cases.input: Write three separate due-diligence findings, one paragraph each, clearly separated by a blank line. Finding 1 facts: passwords are stored in plaintext in the users table. Finding 2 facts: deployments are manual with no rollback procedure. Finding 3 facts: code comment style is inconsistent across the codebase, with no linting rule enforcing a convention.
cases.output:
Passwords are stored in plaintext within the users table, with no hashing or salting applied. Any user with database access can read them directly, and any breach of the database exposes credentials for all accounts. The company has no compensating control. Access to the production database is not restricted to a named set of administrators, and credentials for that access are shared across multiple engineers without audit logging.

Deployments are performed manually via SSH by individual engineers with no documented procedure, no rollback process, and no way to verify what code is currently in production. The most recent production deployment took 45 minutes and required two engineers to coordinate. If a critical bug reaches production, the only remediation is another manual deployment, which carries the same coordination overhead and risk of introducing a further error during the rollback attempt.

Code comment style is inconsistent across the codebase, with no automated enforcement and no style guide referenced in onboarding materials. Comments range from single words to full sentences, use different conventions for TODO and FIXME markers, and include comments in multiple languages. While this does not create a functional defect, it increases friction for engineers onboarding to the codebase and makes it harder to extract and act on technical debt markers during sprints.
